enrichment.whenToUse: Embedded video content, background/hero loops, and camera previews (wire a media stream to `srcObject`). For still pictures use Image. Browsers block unmuted autoplay — combine `autoplay` with `muted` for background video, or start playback from a user action via `play`.

ports.src: String value: URL or project asset path of the video file.
ports.srcObject: MediaStream value; when set, the element plays the stream instead of `src` — used for camera/microphone previews.
ports.play: Signal; resumes playback of the current source.
ports.restart: Signal; seeks to time 0 and plays.
ports.reset: Signal; seeks to time 0 and pauses — 'stop'.
ports.onTimeUpdate: Number value (Playback Position): current playback time in seconds, updated as the video plays.
ports.onCanPlay: Signal; fires when enough data is buffered to start playing — a good moment to reveal the player.
ports.onVideoElementCreated: DOM-element reference to the underlying `video` element, for custom JavaScript integration.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Declared-port-groups: `width`/`height` appear based on `sizeMode`, per-side border width/color ports appear once a border style is chosen, and `pointerEventsEnabled` appears when `pointerEventsMode` is 'explicit'. The playback and event ports are always present.
patterns: Button `onClick` → `play`: user-initiated playback that satisfies browser autoplay policies.
Background hero: `autoplay` + `muted` + `loop` true, `controls` false, `objectFit` 'cover'.
antiPatterns: Expecting `autoplay` alone to start sound-on playback — browsers refuse; either set `muted` or trigger `play` from a user gesture.

inputs.name: action
inputs.description: An action object, an array of them to run in order, or JSON text holding either.

inputs.name: allowedKeys
inputs.description: Comma-separated keys the built-in store actions may write. Blank means any key of the configured store. Setting any key also refuses CLEAR_STORE.

inputs.name: builtIns
inputs.description: Comma-separated built-in action names this dispatcher may execute: SET_STORE, MERGE_STORE, DELETE_STORE_KEY, CLEAR_STORE. Empty — the default — means a server cannot write to the store at all; everything must go through an Action Handler you wired.

inputs.name: channel
inputs.description: Names the handler registry this dispatcher draws on. Leave as "default" unless two independent flows must not see each other.

inputs.name: handlerTimeout
inputs.description: How long a handler has to signal Complete or Fail before the action is failed. 0 waits forever.

inputs.name: maxQueueSize
inputs.description: Bound on queued actions. Overflow refuses the newest so accepted actions keep their order. 0 is unbounded.

inputs.name: rateLimit
inputs.description: Max actions executed per window. 0 is unlimited. Excess actions are refused, not delayed.

inputs.name: storeName
inputs.description: The only store the built-in actions can write. A store named inside an incoming action is ignored — the graph chooses the store, not the server.

inputs.name: waitForHandler
inputs.description: How long an action waits for its handler to appear before being refused as unknown — the window in which a component can still mount. 0 refuses immediately. Everything behind it waits too, because order is preserved.

enrichment.summary: Action Dispatcher: executes actions a backend sent, restricted to a vocabulary this graph explicitly registered.
enrichment.description: Turns messages like `{ "type": "OPEN_SESSION", "sessionId": "123" }` into things that actually happen in the app, so a server-side agent can drive the UI instead of only sending data to display. The vocabulary is **closed**: an action runs only if an Action Handler node registered its type, or it is one of the four built-in store actions (`SET_STORE`, `MERGE_STORE`, `DELETE_STORE_KEY`, `CLEAR_STORE`) and the author listed that name in `builtIns`, which is empty by default. Everything else is refused with a reason on `refusalReason` and a `refused` signal — never silently ignored, and never executed. Actions run strictly one at a time in arrival order, so an array of actions is a multi-step flow; the queue is bounded and overflow refuses the newest rather than reordering what was accepted. An action whose handler has not mounted yet waits up to `waitForHandler` milliseconds rather than losing a mount race, and `waitingFor` names it while it waits.
enrichment.whenToUse: Whenever a backend needs to cause something rather than just report something: an AI agent that says "let me open that for you", a guided tour driven from the server, a workflow whose steps arrive over a stream. Wire a Server-Sent Events or WebSocket node's `data` to `action` and its `onMessage` to `dispatch`. Do not use it as a general message router for data you are simply going to display — wire that straight to its consumer.

ports.channel: Names the handler registry this dispatcher draws on. Only handlers on the same channel are reachable. Leave as `default` unless two independent flows must not see each other.
ports.action: One action object, an array of them to run in order, or JSON text holding either. A frame's raw text works as well as its parsed value.
ports.dispatch: Admits the current action. Acts immediately rather than at end of frame, so several actions arriving in one frame all run instead of coalescing to the last.
ports.cancel: Discards everything queued and abandons anything in flight, reporting the count on `cancelledCount`.
ports.builtIns: Comma-separated built-in action names this dispatcher may execute. Empty — the default — means a server cannot write the store at all. A name that is not a built-in is reported on `lastError` and grants nothing.
ports.storeName: The only store the built-in actions can write. A `storeName` inside an incoming action is ignored: the graph chooses the store, not the server.
ports.allowedKeys: Comma-separated keys the built-in store actions may write. Blank means any key of the configured store. Setting any key also refuses `CLEAR_STORE`, which would remove keys outside the list.
ports.handlerTimeout: How long a handler has to signal Complete or Fail before the action fails and the queue moves on. 0 waits forever.
ports.waitForHandler: How long an action waits for its handler to appear before being refused as unknown. Everything behind it waits too, because order is preserved. 0 refuses immediately.
ports.maxQueueSize: Bound on queued actions; overflow refuses the newest. 0 is unbounded, which a hostile or looping server can grow without limit.
ports.rateLimit: Max actions executed per window; excess is refused, not delayed. 0 is unlimited.
ports.actionType: Type of the action currently executing, or the last one that did.
ports.actionId: The action's `id` if it carried one, else a generated one. Useful for acknowledging back to the server.
ports.payload: The action's `payload`, else its `data`, else the whole action object.
ports.result: What the completing handler or built-in returned.
ports.dispatched: Fires when an action starts executing — after it passed every check.
ports.completed: Fires when an action's handlers all completed.
ports.failed: Fires when a handler failed, threw, or timed out. The action was allowed; it just did not work.
ports.idle: Fires when the queue drains. This is how a multi-step flow knows it finished.
ports.refused: Fires when an action was **not** executed. Wire this — it is the only way an author sees that a server asked for something disallowed.
ports.refusedType: The type that was refused, or empty when the message was too malformed to have one.
ports.refusalMessage: The human-readable reason, safe to show in a debug panel.
ports.lastError: The most recent failure or refusal message.
ports.queueSize: Actions waiting behind the one in flight.
ports.isExecuting: Whether an action is running right now.
ports.waitingFor: The action type held at the head of the queue because no handler has registered for it yet.
ports.completedCount: Actions completed since the node was created.
ports.failedCount: Actions that were allowed but did not work.
ports.refusedCount: Actions refused. A number that climbs unexpectedly means the server and the graph disagree about the vocabulary.

patterns: Server-Sent Events `data` → `action`, `onMessage` → `dispatch`: an agent stream that drives the UI.
One Action Handler per thing the server may do, each wired to the nodes that do it — that set of handlers *is* the permission list, visible on the canvas.
`refusalReason` and `refusalMessage` → a Text node in a debug group: the fastest way to find out that the server is sending `OPEN_VIEW` while the graph registered `OPEN_SESSION`.
Send an array of actions for a guided tour; set `autoComplete` off on the handlers that must finish before the next step starts, and wire `idle` to whatever runs at the end.
Enable `SET_STORE` with `allowedKeys` naming just the view keys the agent may steer, so a store write cannot reach an auth token that happens to live in the same store.

A built-in's own fields may sit on the envelope (`{type:'SET_STORE', key, value}`) or inside `payload` (`{type:'SET_STORE', payload:{key, value}}`) — the same resolution a handler's `payload` output uses, envelope first on a collision. `MERGE_STORE` wants `values` either way. A `storeName` in the message is always ignored in favour of the node's own.
antiPatterns: Enabling built-ins with `allowedKeys` blank on a store that also holds credentials or ids — a server can then overwrite any key in it.
Registering a catch-all handler that reads `payload.command` and switches on it: that re-opens the open vocabulary this node exists to close. One handler per action type.
Leaving `refused` unwired. A dispatcher that refuses everything looks identical to a dead stream if nothing shows the refusals.
Wiring `dispatch` from a signal that fires before `action` is set — the previous action runs again.
Setting `maxQueueSize` to 0 on a stream you do not control.

inputs.name: actionType
inputs.description: The exact action type this handler accepts, e.g. OPEN_SESSION. Registering it is what makes it executable at all.

inputs.name: autoComplete
inputs.description: Report the action complete as soon as Trigger has been sent. Turn off when a later step must wait for this one to finish, and wire Complete or Fail yourself.

inputs.name: channel
inputs.description: Must match the Channel on the Action Dispatcher that should be able to reach this handler.

inputs.name: enabled
inputs.description: Turning this off unregisters the handler, so the action is refused as unknown rather than quietly ignored.

inputs.name: result
inputs.description: Handed back to the dispatcher as the Result of this action when it completes.

enrichment.summary: Action Handler: declares one action type a backend is allowed to trigger, and what happens when it does.
enrichment.description: Registers a single action type with the Action Dispatcher's registry, and fires `trigger` with the action's `payload` whenever a matching action is dispatched. That registration is what makes the action executable at all — there is no separate permission list to keep in step, so an action a graph does not handle simply cannot happen. Registration follows the inputs automatically: no Register signal to remember, and an action that arrives just before the component mounts waits for it rather than being refused. By default the action is reported complete as soon as `trigger` has been sent and everything wired to it has run; turn `autoComplete` off and wire `complete` or `fail` yourself when a later step must wait for this one, or when the step can genuinely fail. Built-in action names (`SET_STORE`, `MERGE_STORE`, `DELETE_STORE_KEY`, `CLEAR_STORE`) are reserved and cannot be claimed here — attempting it reports on `error` and registers nothing.
enrichment.whenToUse: For every action a backend should be able to trigger, one node each. This is also the only way to grant capabilities the dispatcher has no built-in for — navigation, opening a panel, scrolling, showing a toast, refreshing a query — by wiring `trigger` to the nodes that already do those jobs. Be deliberate: whatever is downstream of `trigger` is something a remote server can cause.

ports.channel: Must match the Channel on the Action Dispatcher that should be able to reach this handler.
ports.actionType: The exact type this handler accepts, e.g. `OPEN_SESSION`. Case- and spelling-sensitive; a mismatch shows up as a refusal on the dispatcher, not here.
ports.enabled: Turning this off unregisters the handler, so the action is refused as unknown rather than quietly ignored. Useful for gating an action behind a signed-in state.
ports.autoComplete: Report the action complete as soon as Trigger has been sent. Turn off when a later step must wait for this one, and wire Complete or Fail.
ports.result: Handed back to the dispatcher as its `result` when this action completes.
ports.errorMessage: Handed back to the dispatcher as its `lastError` when Fail is signalled.
ports.complete: Marks the in-flight action done so the next queued action can start. Signalling it with nothing in flight reports on `error`.
ports.fail: Marks the in-flight action failed. The dispatcher fires `failed` and moves on.
ports.trigger: Fires when a matching action is dispatched. The payload is already set when it fires.
ports.payload: The action's `payload`, else its `data`, else the whole action object — so `{type, sessionId}` gives you an object with `sessionId` on it.
ports.actionId: The dispatched action's id, for correlating an acknowledgement back to the server.
ports.registered: Whether this handler is currently in the registry. False means the action cannot run at all.
ports.triggeredCount: How many times this handler has run.
ports.error: Why registration failed, or that Complete/Fail was signalled with nothing in flight.

patterns: `trigger` → Navigate, `payload` → Set Variable: the server can open a screen. A real capability, granted visibly by this one wire.

`autoComplete` off, `trigger` → a cloud function call, its Success → `complete` and Failure → `fail`: the dispatcher then holds the rest of the flow until the call returns, and reports the failure if it does not.
`enabled` driven from a signed-in flag, so an action becomes reachable only once the user is authenticated.
Two handlers with the same `actionType` both run, in registration order — useful for a shared side effect such as logging every occurrence of one action.
antiPatterns: One handler with a generic type such as `RUN`, switching on a field of the payload. That rebuilds the open vocabulary the dispatcher closed; the refusal path then never fires for anything.
Leaving `autoComplete` on for a step a later step depends on — the flow moves to the next action while this one is still working.
Turning `autoComplete` off and forgetting to wire `complete`: the action sits until the dispatcher's `handlerTimeout` and fails.
Wiring `trigger` to something destructive without any confirmation in between.

dynamicPorts.description: Property ports are created from the "properties" parameter (the schema of the component object).

variables.property: one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter
one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter

enrichment.summary: Component Object: per-component-instance shared state — every node in the same instance reads and writes the same object, no wires needed.
enrichment.description: Component Object exposes an object that belongs to the component *instance* it sits in: each instance of the component gets its own backing object, created on first use, and all Component Object nodes inside that instance — plus Parent Component Object nodes in child components — see the same data. Property names are declared in the `properties` parameter; each becomes a connection-only port that is both readable and writable, together with a per-property changed signal. By default outputs are push-style: whenever the object changes (from this node, another Component Object node, a Set Component Object Properties node, or a child's Parent Component Object), the value outputs update and the changed signals fire. Connecting the `fetch` input switches the node to pull mode: outputs then refresh only when `fetch` fires, followed by `fetched`.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it for state shared across nodes within one component — form drafts, wizard step, selection — especially state a child component must also see via Parent Component Object. It is per-instance by design: two instances of the component never share data. For app-global state use a Variable (Variable2) or Object (Model2); for a fixed set of visual modes prefer States.

ports.fetch: Signal input; when connected, the node stops pushing on every change and instead refreshes all property outputs (and fires the changed signals and `fetched`) only when this fires.
ports.changed: Signal; fires whenever any property of the instance's object changes (push mode).
ports.properties: Edit-only stringlist declaring the object's property names; each becomes a `value-<name>` port and a `changed-<name>` signal.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior:
Ports are runtime-discovered from the `properties` parameter: each declared name p produces `value-

` — a connection-only, any-type port usable both as input (writing stores the value into the instance's object) and as output (reading the current value) — and a `changed-

` signal output that fires when that property changes. The ports do not exist until `properties` is set; an authoring tool must write the `properties` stringlist and may then connect `value-

`/`changed-

` by those exact names.
patterns: Component Object in the parent + Parent Component Object in children: parent↔child shared state without threading Component Inputs/Outputs through every level.
Inside a Repeater item component: per-row UI state (expanded, editing) — each item instance automatically gets its own object.
antiPatterns: Using it as global app state — every instance has a separate object, so two sibling components' Component Objects never see each other. Use Variables or Objects instead.
Writing a property and expecting the paired output on the same node to be a different value — input and output are two faces of the same stored property.

enrichment.summary: Declares a named observable store and outputs its state, so any component can read shared state without prop drilling.
enrichment.description: Creates (or attaches to) a named store and keeps `state` in step with it. A store is backed by the runtime's own Model, keyed `--ndl--global-store--<name>`, which is the same mechanism Variables already use — so a store is visible to Function nodes and `Noodl.Object`, and a write made directly to the backing Model notifies store subscribers exactly as Set Global Store does. Any number of Global Store nodes may name the same store; they all observe one shared object rather than each holding a copy. Notifications fire once per commit, not once per key: writes inside a batch collapse into a single `stateChanged`, and `changedKeys` lists only keys whose value actually differs — setting a key to the value it already held reports nothing. Re-entrant writes made from a subscriber are queued and applied rather than recursed, so a subscriber that writes cannot deepen the stack. Deleting the node releases its subscription.
enrichment.whenToUse: State more than one component needs: the signed-in user, a theme, a cart, an agent conversation, the open panel. Reach for it instead of threading Component Inputs down a tree or wiring a Send Event to every interested component. For state that belongs to one component, Variables and Component Object are simpler and stay local. For a value that must survive a reload, turn on Persist rather than writing your own storage step.

ports.storeName: Names the store. Two nodes with the same name share one object; change the name and the node moves to a different store rather than renaming the old one.
ports.initialState: Fills in keys the store does not yet have. It never overwrites live state, so a component that remounts cannot reset a store other components are using.
ports.persist: Saves the store and restores it on the next load. Persistence goes through an injected storage seam, and an unavailable or full store is reported on Error rather than silently skipped.
ports.storageKey: Where a persisted store is written. Defaults to a key derived from Store Name; set it explicitly when two projects share an origin.
ports.state: The whole store object. Updates once per commit.
ports.changedKeys: The keys that actually changed in the commit that just fired — the cheap way to react to one key without comparing whole objects.
ports.stateChanged: Fires once per commit, after State has updated.
ports.ready: True once the store exists and any persisted state has been read back, so a graph can wait rather than reading an empty store on the first frame.
ports.error: Carries persistence and subscriber failures. A subscriber that throws is isolated and reported here rather than taking down the other subscribers.
ports.storeId: The id of the backing Model, for wiring the store into nodes that take a Model reference.

patterns: One Global Store node per component that needs to read shared state; there is no 'owner' node to place first, because naming the store creates it.
`changedKeys` → a condition, rather than watching `state` and diffing by hand, when only one key matters.
Set Global Store with Batch With Others turned on for several related writes, so the UI updates once rather than flickering through intermediate states.
Wait on `ready` before reading a persisted store, instead of reading on the first frame and getting a store that has not loaded yet.
antiPatterns: Using a store for state only one component reads — Variables and Component Object are simpler and do not outlive the component.
Setting Initial State from several components expecting the last one to win: it fills gaps only and never overwrites, by design.
Treating `state` as a snapshot to hold on to. It is the live object; use the State History node if you need to keep earlier values.

enrichment.summary: Writes a key into a named global store, optionally merging an object and optionally batching with other writes in the same frame.
enrichment.description: Sets one key in the store named by Store Name. The write is deferred until every input on the node has landed, because Key, Value and the Set signal can arrive in one frame in no guaranteed order — so wiring Value and pulsing Set together behaves the way it reads. Setting a key to the value it already holds is not a change and notifies nobody. Writing `undefined` to a key that does not exist still registers as setting it, so absence and 'set to nothing' stay distinguishable to anything watching. Batch With Others coalesces this write with the other batched writes of the same frame into a single commit — subscribers see one notification with all the changed keys, instead of one per write.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any write to shared state: recording a sign-in, appending a streamed message, flipping a panel open. Use one Set per key; for several keys that belong together, turn on Batch With Others so the UI moves once. Use Merge Object to update part of an object without reading it first.

ports.storeName: Which store to write to. Writing to a name no Global Store node declares still creates the store — the store exists because it is named, not because a node owns it.
ports.key: The key to write. Required; an empty key reports on Error rather than writing something unnamed.
ports.value: The value to write. Any type, including objects, arrays, Models and Collections.
ports.merge: Merges Value into the existing object at Key instead of replacing it. With no existing object it behaves as a plain set.
ports.transaction: Batches this write with the other batched writes of the same frame into one commit, so subscribers get a single notification. It does not skip or suppress the notification — the change is always delivered.
ports.completed: Fires after the write has been committed, so a chained action runs against the new state rather than the old.
ports.error: Carries a refused write — a missing key, or a store that could not be persisted — instead of failing quietly.

patterns: Several Set Global Store nodes with Batch With Others turned on, pulsed in the same frame, so a multi-field update renders as one change.
Merge Object to update one field of a settings object without reading, spreading and writing it back.
`completed` → the next action, rather than assuming the write has landed by the time the next node runs.
antiPatterns: Expecting Batch With Others to hide a change. It groups notifications; it never drops the write.
Setting the same key from several nodes each frame and relying on order — batched writes commit together, and last-write-wins within the batch.
Writing a whole rebuilt object every keystroke where Merge Object would change one field.

inputs.name: keys
inputs.description: Comma-separated keys to watch. Leave blank to react to every change in the store.

enrichment.summary: Watches specific keys in a named global store and signals when they change, with the previous value alongside the new one.
enrichment.description: Subscribes to a store and fires only for the keys named in Keys, so a component that cares about one field is not woken by every unrelated write. Leaving Keys empty watches the whole store. Both Value and Previous Value update before `changed` fires, so a handler can compare them. Notifications arrive once per commit in subscriber registration order; a write that sets a key to the value it already held is not a change and fires nothing. Changing Store Name or Keys moves the subscription rather than adding a second one, and deleting the node removes it — a disposed node leaves no subscriber behind, which matters because a store outlives the components that read it.
enrichment.whenToUse: Reacting to shared state changing, rather than rendering it. To display a value, wire Global Store's `state` straight into the UI; use Subscribe when something must *happen* on a change — refetch, animate, navigate, log. Prefer naming Keys over watching everything, so unrelated writes do not trigger work.

ports.storeName: Which store to watch. The store need not exist yet; the subscription attaches when it appears.
ports.keys: Comma-separated keys to watch. Empty watches every key in the store.
ports.value: The current value of the changed key, or the whole store object when Keys is empty.
ports.previousValue: What that key held immediately before this change — the two are updated together so they can be compared in a handler.
ports.changedKeys: Which of the watched keys changed in this commit. A batched write can change several at once, and they arrive in one notification.
ports.changed: Fires once per commit that touched a watched key, after Value and Previous Value have updated.

patterns: Name the keys you care about instead of leaving Keys empty, so a busy store does not wake every component on every write.
Compare `previousValue` with `value` to react to a specific transition — signed-out to signed-in — rather than to any change at all.
Global Store `state` for rendering; Subscribe `changed` for side effects. Using Subscribe to drive display work is usually a sign the state should simply be wired in.
antiPatterns: Watching the whole store to react to one key: every unrelated write then does that component's work again.
Expecting one notification per key when several were written in a batch — a batch is one commit, and `changedKeys` names all of them.
Holding `previousValue` as a history. It is only the value immediately before this change; the State History node keeps a real history.

dynamicPorts.description: Input and output ports derive from node parameters: configured headers and query parameters become inputs; response mappings become outputs.

parameterEncoding.reason: Ports are parsed from the configured headers, query parameters and response mappings in the node parameters.

enrichment.summary: HTTP Request: fetches a URL on demand, delivering the parsed response, status code and success/failure signals.
enrichment.description: The straightforward HTTP client: set `url` (plus method/headers/body via its configuration), fire `fetch`, and read `response` (parsed body, untyped), `responseHeaders`, and `statusCode`. `success`/`failure` split the outcome, with `error` describing failures; `cancel` aborts an in-flight request.
enrichment.whenToUse: One-off or simple API calls where the response can be consumed directly or handed to a Function/Script for shaping. Prefer the REST node when an endpoint is reused enough to deserve declared ports; prefer a cloud function when credentials must stay off the client.

ports.response: Untyped output with the parsed body — being '*', it connects anywhere; downstream correctness is on the author.
ports.statusCode: Number level with the HTTP status of the last response.
ports.failure: Signal; wire error display/retry here, with `error` carrying the message.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Header and body inputs are runtime-registered from the node's method/headers configuration; only the core trigger/result surface is static.
patterns: `failure` → Condition `eval` with `result` → error text `visible`: errors as levels, not pulses.

inputs.name: maxLength
inputs.description: Cap on unparsed text held while waiting for a value to complete. Exceeding it clears the buffer and reports an error, rather than growing without limit on a malformed stream.

enrichment.summary: JSON Stream Parser: turns stream fragments into JSON values as NDJSON, concatenated values, or one whole document.
enrichment.description: Each `parse` appends the current `chunk` to a buffer and extracts whatever is now complete. 'NDJSON' takes one value per line and reports a line that does not parse rather than skipping it silently. 'Stream' accepts any concatenation of complete top-level values — whitespace-separated objects, or a JSON array whose elements are emitted as they close — and is safe at every chunk boundary, including one that falls inside a string. 'Single document' holds everything back until the whole buffer is one complete value, then emits it. Text that is not yet a complete value stays in the buffer and shows on `pendingCharacters`; `maxLength` stops a malformed stream from growing without bound by clearing the buffer and reporting it. `values` carries everything the last parse completed, `parsed` the last of them.
enrichment.whenToUse: A stream whose payloads are JSON but do not arrive one-per-event: NDJSON logs, a chunked HTTP body, an array streamed element by element. Not needed for Server-Sent Events with one JSON object per event — that node already parses each payload onto its Data output.

ports.chunk: The fragment to append. Empty chunks are ignored, so a Parse with nothing new re-tries the existing buffer.
ports.format: 'NDJSON' for line-delimited, 'Stream' for concatenated values and streamed arrays, 'Single document' to wait for one whole value.
ports.maxLength: Cap on unparsed text. Exceeding it clears the buffer and reports an error, which almost always means the wrong Format.
ports.parsed: The last value completed by the most recent Parse.
ports.values: Every value completed by the most recent Parse, in order. Wire this to For Each when a chunk can complete several.
ports.valueCount: Running total across all parses, not the size of the last batch.
ports.pendingCharacters: Text held back because a value is incomplete. Persistently non-zero means the Format does not match the stream.
ports.isComplete: True when the last Parse left nothing buffered.
ports.success: Fires only when the Parse produced at least one value, so an advancing-but-incomplete chunk stays quiet.
ports.failure: Fires per malformed value; the stream keeps going rather than stalling on one bad record.

patterns: Server-Sent Events `data` → `chunk`, `onMessage` → `parse`, format NDJSON: a log stream that arrives several lines per event.
`values` → For Each `items` renders everything a chunk completed, instead of only the last value.
`pendingCharacters` on a debug Text output makes a format mismatch obvious instead of looking like a dead stream.
antiPatterns: Using 'Single document' on a never-ending stream — the buffer grows until Max Pending trips.
Reading only `parsed` when a chunk can complete several values; the earlier ones are then silently ignored.
Adding this after Server-Sent Events when each event is already one JSON object — the SSE node's Data output has parsed it.

inputs.name: errorMessage
inputs.description: Reason reported on Error when this update is rolled back. Wire the server error here.

inputs.name: onDispose
inputs.description: What happens to updates still in flight when this node is removed. Rolling back keeps the store honest; keeping the value suits fire-and-forget actions the user navigates away from.

inputs.name: timeout
inputs.description: Roll back automatically after this long with no answer. Zero disables the deadline.

inputs.name: transactionId
inputs.description: Leave blank to let the node generate one. Set it to commit or roll back a specific update when several are in flight.

enrichment.summary: Writes a store key immediately, then commits or rolls it back when the server answers — so the UI responds now, not after the round trip.
enrichment.description: Applies `optimisticValue` to `key` the moment Apply fires, and holds the change open until Commit or Rollback resolves it. A rollback restores what was there before, and restores *absence as absence* — a key the update introduced is deleted rather than left holding `undefined`. Several updates can be open at once, each with its own transaction id and its own deadline. Two behaviours are worth knowing before relying on it. First, if a plain write changes the same key while an update is open, rollback **keeps the newer value**: `rolledBack` still fires so the failure branch runs, and `error` explains that the value was left alone, because silently reverting a write the user made after the fact is worse than a stale optimistic value. A newer *optimistic* update is not treated as supersession — the store's own newest-writer rule already resolves that correctly. Second, disposal resolves rather than leaks: a node deleted with updates still open rolls them back by default (or commits them, under On Dispose), clears its timers, and fires nothing into the dead node.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any action where waiting on the network makes the UI feel slow and the write is very likely to succeed: toggling a like, accepting an invite, checking off a task, reordering a list. Do not use it where a wrong-then-corrected value would mislead — a bank balance, a booking confirmation, a payment state. There, a pending indicator is the honest option.

ports.storeName: The store to write to. Defaults to `app`.
ports.key: The key held open by this update.
ports.optimisticValue: The value shown immediately, before the server has agreed to it.
ports.errorMessage: The message reported on Error if the update rolls back. Set it to the server's reason when you have one.
ports.transactionId: Identifies this update, so several in flight can be committed or rolled back individually. Left empty, one is generated and reported on the output of the same name.
ports.timeout: Milliseconds before the update rolls itself back. Default 30000; 0 disables it. A deadline matters here — without one, a request that never answers leaves the optimistic value on screen forever.
ports.onDispose: What an open update does when the node is deleted: roll back (the default, and the safe reading) or commit.
ports.apply: Applies the optimistic value and opens the update.
ports.commit: Confirms the update. The value stays and the update closes.
ports.rollback: Rejects the update, restoring the previous value unless a newer plain write superseded it.
ports.value: The current value of the key.
ports.previousValue: What the key held before this update, i.e. what a rollback would restore.
ports.isPending: True while at least one update from this node is open.
ports.pendingCount: How many updates from this node are open — the number to show as 'saving'.
ports.timedOut: Fires when an update rolled back because its deadline passed rather than because the server rejected it. Fires after `rolledBack`.
ports.error: Carries the rollback reason, including the explanation when a newer write was kept in preference to reverting it.

patterns: Apply on the click, Commit on the request's success, Rollback on its failure — with `errorMessage` wired from the server's reason so the message the user sees is the real one.
`pendingCount` → a subtle 'saving' indicator, rather than a blocking spinner: the point of the pattern is that the UI already moved.
Leave `transactionId` empty and read the output when several updates can be in flight, instead of inventing ids by hand.
antiPatterns: Using it for state where being briefly wrong misleads — money, confirmations, availability. Optimism is a UX choice about likely-successful writes, not a way to avoid showing pending state.
Setting `timeout` to 0 on a network call: a request that never answers then leaves the optimistic value on screen permanently.
Expecting Rollback to always restore the old value. If the user changed the key in the meantime, their write is kept and `error` says so.

dynamicPorts.description: Property ports mirror the parent component object's property schema.

variables.property: one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter
one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter

enrichment.summary: Parent Component Object: reads the enclosing parent component's instance-scoped object from inside a child component.
enrichment.description: Parent Component Object opens the same per-instance store as the parent's Component Object, from within a child. Properties declared on the node become value outputs that update reactively as anything writes the parent's object; `changed` fires per write. This is how reusable child components (controls, toolbars, wizard steps) participate in their host's state without dedicated ports for every value.
enrichment.whenToUse: Child components that are conceptually part of their parent and share its state — wizard controls, list toolbars. For unrelated components use Objects by id or events; for one-off values a Component Input is more explicit.

ports.properties: Declared property names; each becomes a reactive value output.
ports.changed: Signal; the parent's object was written by anyone.
ports.fetch: Signal; re-emit current values on demand.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Property ports are generated from the per-instance `properties` list (runtime-discovered). Resolution walks up to the nearest ancestor component instance — the node is inert at the app root.

inputs.name: flags
inputs.description: Regex flags: i (ignore case), m (multiline), s (dot matches newline), u (unicode). g is controlled by Extract All.

inputs.name: pattern
inputs.description: A JavaScript regular expression, without the surrounding slashes. Capture groups appear on Groups.

enrichment.summary: Pattern Extractor: pulls matches and capture groups out of text with a regular expression, without needing a Function node.
enrichment.description: Runs `pattern` over `text` on each `extract` and publishes the first match, its capture groups (numbered and named), and — with Extract All on — every match. An optional group that did not participate becomes an empty string rather than a hole in the array, so downstream indexes stay stable. `firstGroup` is a convenience for the overwhelmingly common single-group case. A pattern that will not compile is a result, not an exception: `ok` becomes false, `error` explains, and the `failure` signal fires — distinct from `notFound`, which is a normal outcome. Note that a catastrophically backtracking pattern is still the author's problem; this runs the platform regex engine and cannot bound it.
enrichment.whenToUse: Extracting a value from text that is not structured data: a percentage out of a progress line, a tool name out of an agent status message, a field out of a log record. Prefer JSON Stream Parser when the payload really is JSON, and String Format or Substring for fixed-position work that needs no pattern.

ports.text: The text to search. Non-strings are stringified, since stream payloads are typed `*`.
ports.pattern: A JavaScript regular expression without the surrounding slashes.
ports.flags: i, m, s, u. The global flag is controlled by Extract All and is stripped from here, so `match` cannot become stateful across calls.
ports.extractAll: Collect every match rather than only the first. Groups still describe the first match.
ports.match: The first match, or an empty string when nothing matched.
ports.groups: Numbered capture groups of the first match; unmatched optional groups are empty strings.
ports.firstGroup: Group 1 of the first match — the value you want in the common `(\d+)%` case.
ports.namedGroups: Named capture groups of the first match, as an object.
ports.error: Empty unless the pattern would not compile.
ports.found: Fires when there was a match.
ports.notFound: Fires when the pattern compiled but matched nothing — a normal outcome, not an error.
ports.failure: Fires only when the pattern itself is unusable, so a broken pattern cannot hide as 'no match'.

patterns: Stream text → `text`, pattern `(\d+)%`, `firstGroup` → Number → a progress bar.
Named groups turn one pattern into several outputs without chaining extractors: `(?<tool>\w+)\s+(?<state>\w+)`.
`failure` → a visible warning during authoring catches a mistyped pattern that would otherwise read as 'never matches'.
antiPatterns: Parsing JSON with a regex instead of using JSON Stream Parser.
Treating `notFound` as an error state — most streams contain lines the pattern is not meant to match.
Building a pattern from user input without bounding it; nested quantifiers can hang the frame.

ssr.note: An event stream cannot be consumed during a server render; the node connects in the browser after hydration.

inputs.name: dedupeById
inputs.description: Drop events whose id has already been seen, so a reconnect that resumes from the last event id cannot re-deliver messages. Turn off if your server reuses ids for distinct events.

inputs.name: eventTypes
inputs.description: Comma-separated named event types to subscribe to. Only needed for the EventSource transport, which delivers a named event only to a listener registered in advance; the Fetch transport delivers every event type.

inputs.name: maxRetries
inputs.description: 0 means keep retrying. Otherwise the connection reports an error after this many consecutive failures.

inputs.name: reconnectDelay
inputs.description: First retry delay. Doubles per consecutive failure, up to the maximum.

inputs.name: reconnectOnStreamEnd
inputs.description: Reconnect when the server closes the stream cleanly. Off by default: an agent response stream is finite, and reconnecting would re-issue the request and start the response again.

inputs.name: textPath
inputs.description: Where the text lives inside a JSON payload, as a dot path — for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, choices.0.delta.content. Leave blank for a stream that sends bare text. Whatever it names ends up on the Text output, which is always a string.

enrichment.summary: Server-Sent Events: consumes a streaming HTTP endpoint, with connection state, retries and errors as graph outputs.
enrichment.description: Opens a `text/event-stream` connection and turns each event into outputs plus an `onMessage` signal. Two transports: Fetch (the default under 'Auto') can send headers, a method and a body, receives every event type, resumes with an explicit `Last-Event-ID`, and can tell a finished stream from a dropped one; EventSource is the browser's own client, which cannot set headers or POST, needs named event types declared up front on `eventTypes`, and reconnects on its own schedule. Failures never disappear: `connectionState` moves through idle/connecting/open/reconnecting/closed/error, `retryCount` counts consecutive failures, `lastError` carries the message and `onError` fires. Retries use exponential backoff from `reconnectDelay` up to `maxReconnectDelay`, honouring a server `retry:` field when one arrives. A 4xx is terminal (retrying cannot help); 5xx, 408 and 429 are retried. Deleting the node or navigating away aborts the request and clears every timer.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any server-push stream: AI/agent responses streamed token by token, progress on a long-running job, live notifications, dashboard metrics. Use the Fetch transport whenever the endpoint needs an Authorization header or a request body — the usual shape for an AI backend. Use REST2 or HTTP Request for ordinary request/response, and a WebSocket node when the client must also send on the same connection. Client-only: the node stays inert during server-side rendering and connects after hydration.

ports.url: Stream endpoint. Required before Connect does anything; an empty URL reports an error rather than failing silently.
ports.transport: 'Auto' picks Fetch wherever fetch exists. Choose 'EventSource' only to get the browser's own reconnection behaviour.
ports.method: Fetch transport only. POST is the common case for an AI endpoint that takes a prompt.
ports.headers: Fetch transport only — an object of header name to value. EventSource cannot send headers at all.
ports.body: Fetch transport only. An object is JSON-encoded and Content-Type is set unless Headers already sets it.
ports.eventTypes: Comma-separated named event types. Only needed for EventSource, which delivers a named event only to a listener registered in advance.
ports.textPath: Where the text lives inside a JSON payload, as a dot path — `choices.0.delta.content` for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Blank for a stream that sends bare text. Whatever it names appears on `text`.
ports.autoConnect: Connects once the URL and the rest of the inputs have landed, without needing a Connect signal.
ports.autoReconnect: Retry after a failure. Off means a single failure goes straight to the error state.
ports.reconnectOnStreamEnd: Off by default. An agent response stream is finite, and reconnecting would re-issue the request and start the response again.
ports.maxRetries: 0 keeps retrying. Otherwise the connection reports an error naming the budget it spent.
ports.dedupeById: Drops events whose id was already seen, so a resumed reconnect cannot re-deliver messages. Turn off only if the server reuses ids for distinct events.
ports.connectionState: idle, connecting, open, reconnecting, closed or error. 'error' is terminal; 'reconnecting' means another attempt is coming.
ports.connected: True only while the stream is open — false during connect, backoff and after a terminal failure.
ports.data: The event payload, parsed as JSON when it parses and left as the raw string when it does not (so a `[DONE]` sentinel arrives intact). An *object* for a JSON payload — feed a Text node or a Text Accumulator from `text`, not from here.
ports.raw: The payload exactly as sent, before any JSON parsing.
ports.text: The one data output that is always a string: the payload as sent when `textPath` is blank, or the field at that path when it is set. A missing field, a non-JSON sentinel or a path landing on an object all read as empty rather than as `[object Object]`.
ports.eventType: The `event:` field of the last event, or 'message' when the server sent none.
ports.lastEventId: The furthest `id:` the server has sent; this is what a reconnect resumes from.
ports.deliverySemantics: 'at-most-once' when the server sends no ids (gap events are lost), 'at-least-once' when it does, 'at-least-once-deduped' when ids are present and Dedupe By Id is on.
ports.duplicatesSuppressed: How many replayed events were dropped after a resume. Non-zero is normal after a reconnect.
ports.onMessage: Fires once per event, after the Data outputs have updated — so an accumulator wired `text` → `chunk` and `onMessage` → `add` sees the chunk first.
ports.onClose: Fires when the stream stops, whether cleanly or with a terminal error, so a Close handler always runs.
ports.onError: Fires on every failure, including ones the node is about to retry.

patterns: SSE `text` → Text Accumulator `chunk` and SSE `onMessage` → Text Accumulator `add`, with an empty delimiter, renders an AI response as it is written. Set `textPath` to `choices.0.delta.content` for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and leave it blank for a stream of bare tokens; either way `text` is a string.
`data` is for the payloads that are meant to be objects: a JSON Stream Parser, or an Action Dispatcher's `action` input.
SSE `connectionState` → String Mapper → a status label makes reconnection visible instead of leaving the UI apparently frozen.
POST the prompt in `body` with an Authorization header rather than putting a token in the query string, which the EventSource-only approach forces.
antiPatterns: Turning on Reconnect On Stream End for a finite agent response — the request is re-issued and the answer regenerates in a loop.
Ignoring `connectionState` and wiring only the data outputs: a silently failing reconnection then looks identical to a slow server.

Wiring `data` into anything that expects text. `data` is JSON-parsed, so for the commonest agent shape (`data: {"delta":"Hi"}`) it is an object; a Text Accumulator refuses it and reports the mis-wiring rather than appending `[object Object]`. Use `text`.
Leaving `textPath` blank on a JSON-envelope stream and wiring `raw` instead — the answer then reads as a run of JSON fragments.
Using the EventSource transport when the endpoint needs an Authorization header, then smuggling the token through the URL.

dynamicPorts.description: Property input ports follow the "properties" parameter.

variables.property: one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter
one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter

enrichment.summary: Set Component Object Properties: writes declared values onto this component instance's own object when store fires.
enrichment.description: The writing half of Component Object: property values set on this node's declared inputs are committed to the enclosing component instance's object when `store` fires, and every Component Object / Parent Component Object reader of that instance sees the change immediately. `stored` confirms the write.
enrichment.whenToUse: Mutating instance-scoped state: resetting a wizard, recording a selection local to this instance. For state shared across instances or screens use Objects (Model2) or Variables instead.

ports.properties: Declared property names; each becomes a value input written on store.
ports.store: Signal; commits the current input values to the instance's object.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Property inputs are generated from the per-instance `properties` list (runtime-discovered).

dynamicPorts.description: Property input ports follow the "properties" parameter.

variables.property: one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter
one of the comma-separated entries in the `properties` parameter

enrichment.summary: Set Parent Component Object Properties: writes declared values onto the enclosing parent component's object from a child.
enrichment.description: The child-side writer for a parent's instance state: values on the declared property inputs are committed to the nearest ancestor component instance's object when `store` fires, updating every reader of that object (the parent's Component Object, sibling children's Parent Component Object). `stored` confirms.
enrichment.whenToUse: Child components that advance or edit their host's state — 'next step' controls, embedded editors. Keep writes coarse (one store per user action); each store fans out to all readers.

ports.properties: Declared property names; each becomes a value input written on store.
ports.store: Signal; commits to the parent instance's object.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Property inputs are generated from the per-instance `properties` list (runtime-discovered); resolution targets the nearest ancestor component instance.

inputs.name: coalesceMs
inputs.description: Fold successive changes to the same keys within this many milliseconds into one undo step, so typing is one undo rather than one per keystroke. 0 records every change separately.

inputs.name: enabled
inputs.description: Turning this off pauses recording. The history already collected is kept.

inputs.name: maxHistory
inputs.description: How many entries to keep. The oldest are dropped first. An unbounded history is a memory leak.

inputs.name: trackKeys
inputs.description: Comma-separated keys to record. Blank records the whole store. Undo then writes only these keys and leaves the rest alone. Changing this clears the history.

enrichment.summary: Records a bounded history of a store's state so it can be undone, redone or stepped through, and reports what it cannot fully restore.
enrichment.description: Watches a store and records an entry per commit, keeping `entries[currentIndex]` always equal to live state. History is bounded by `maxHistory` (default 50): the oldest entry is dropped first, never the current one, and lowering the bound while you are mid-travel drops the redo tail instead. A new write truncates the redo stack, as undo/redo everywhere does. An undo is an ordinary store commit — every other subscriber sees it as a normal change, not a special replay — so nothing in the graph needs to know time travel exists. Where it is honest rather than magical: values that can only be captured by reference (Models, Collections, functions, cyclic objects) are *not* deep-copied, so undoing does not restore their internal state. `fullyRestorable` and `byReferenceKeys` say exactly which keys those are, rather than letting the feature quietly under-deliver. Coalescing (`coalesceMs`, off by default) folds rapid same-key writes into one entry so undo steps match user intent instead of keystrokes — and never folds into the entry a navigation just landed on, which would destroy the state you had just undone to.
enrichment.whenToUse: Undo/redo over shared state — a form, an editor, a builder, a drawing surface — and stepping back through state while debugging. Place one per store you want tracked; wire the Undo / Redo node to the buttons. For a single named checkpoint rather than a moving history, use State Snapshot. Check `fullyRestorable` before advertising undo over state that holds Collections or Models.

ports.storeName: The store to track. Tracking is reference-counted, so a second State History node on the same store does not wipe the first one's history.
ports.trackKeys: Comma-separated keys to track; empty tracks the whole store. Only tracked keys are restored, so a filtered history leaves everything else alone.
ports.maxHistory: Entries kept, default 50, floor 2. This is a memory bound: an unbounded history in a long-running app grows without limit.
ports.coalesceMs: Window in which consecutive writes to the same keys fold into one entry. 0 (default) records every commit separately. Set it to roughly a typing pause when undo should step by word rather than by character.
ports.enabled: False pauses recording without discarding history. Resuming records an entry if state drifted while paused, so the history never claims a change did not happen.
ports.clearHistory: Discards every entry and starts again from live state.
ports.currentIndex: Where in the history live state sits. Not at the end means you are mid-travel and a new write will truncate the redo tail.
ports.canUndo: Whether an earlier entry exists — wire it to the Undo button's enabled state rather than guessing.
ports.fullyRestorable: False when any tracked key in the history could only be captured by reference, so undo cannot fully restore it.
ports.byReferenceKeys: Which keys those are. Show this rather than letting an author believe undo is total.
ports.history: Entry descriptors (not the states themselves) for building a timeline UI, each flagged with whether it is partial.
ports.historyChanged: Fires when an entry is added, dropped, or the current position moves.

patterns: `canUndo`/`canRedo` → the buttons' enabled state, so the affordance matches reality.
`coalesceMs` around 300–500 for text input, so an undo removes a word rather than a letter.
`history` → a Repeater for a visible timeline, with `currentIndex` marking where you are.
Surface `byReferenceKeys` in a developer-facing view when the store holds Collections, instead of discovering the limit through a confusing undo.
antiPatterns: Leaving `maxHistory` unbounded-by-intent in a long-running app: every entry is retained state.
Assuming undo restores everything. A key listed in `byReferenceKeys` shares its object with the entry, so its internal state was never copied.
Tracking the whole store when only a form's keys need undoing — unrelated writes then become undo steps the user did not make.

enrichment.summary: Moves a store backwards, forwards, or to a specific point in the history recorded by a State History node.
enrichment.description: Drives the history that a State History node on the same store is recording; it records nothing itself, so a store with no State History node has nothing to undo and says so on Error rather than failing quietly. Undo and Redo step one entry; Jump To moves straight to `targetIndex`, which is what a timeline UI needs. Each move is an ordinary store commit, so subscribers and bindings update exactly as they do for any other change. After every move, `fullyRestorable` and `byReferenceKeys` describe *the restore that just happened* — not the whole history — so an author can tell the user when a particular step could not be fully reversed instead of leaving them to notice.
enrichment.whenToUse: Wire it to Undo and Redo buttons, a keyboard shortcut, or a timeline UI. One node can serve all three: Undo, Redo and Jump To are separate signals on the same node. Take the buttons' enabled state from the State History node's `canUndo`/`canRedo` rather than from here.

ports.storeName: The store to move. A State History node must already be tracking it.
ports.targetIndex: Where Jump To goes. Out-of-range values are reported on Error rather than clamped silently, so a broken timeline UI is visible.
ports.redo: Steps forward one entry. Nothing happens if a write has since truncated the redo tail.
ports.jumped: Fires after a successful Jump To.
ports.fullyRestorable: Whether the restore that just happened was complete. False means some key could only be restored by reference.
ports.byReferenceKeys: Which keys in the restore that just happened could not be deep-restored.
ports.error: Carries the reason a move did nothing: no history for that store, nothing to undo or redo, or an out-of-range target.

patterns: State History `canUndo` → the Undo button's enabled state, and this node's `undo` → its click. The recording node owns the availability; this one owns the action.
`jumpTo` with `targetIndex` from a Repeater index, for a clickable timeline.
Show `byReferenceKeys` after a move where `fullyRestorable` is false, rather than leaving the user to discover the gap.
antiPatterns: Expecting it to work without a State History node on the same store — it drives a history, it does not keep one.
Wiring Undo to a button whose enabled state ignores `canUndo`: the button then does nothing at the end of the history.
Treating a failed move as impossible. Read `error` — out-of-range jumps and truncated redo tails are both normal.

inputs.name: snapshotData
inputs.description: Snapshot to restore instead of the named one — a previously exported "Snapshot" output. Leave blank to restore by name.

enrichment.summary: Saves a named snapshot of a store and restores it later — a checkpoint, rather than the moving history State History keeps.
enrichment.description: Save captures the store as it is now; Restore writes it back as a single commit that subscribers see as an ordinary change. A snapshot is copied in on restore, so **the same snapshot can be restored any number of times** — which is what makes it usable as a reset point rather than a one-shot. `snapshot` outputs the captured value, and `snapshotData` accepts one back, so a snapshot can be round-tripped through JSON: persisted, sent to a server, or restored in another session. As with State History, values that could only be captured by reference are not deep-copied, and `fullyRestorable` / `byReferenceKeys` name them rather than letting the checkpoint quietly under-deliver. Errors are reported on the Error output instead of thrown out of a signal handler.
enrichment.whenToUse: A discrete checkpoint: 'reset this form', 'revert to the last saved version', 'restore the state I shipped this bug report with'. Use State History instead when you want undo/redo over every change; use this when you want one or two named points you return to deliberately. The `snapshot`/`snapshotData` pair is also the straightforward way to persist state across sessions or attach it to a bug report.

ports.storeName: The store to capture or restore.
ports.snapshotName: A label for the snapshot, so several checkpoints are distinguishable in a UI.
ports.snapshotData: A snapshot captured earlier, fed back in to be restored — the input side of the round trip through JSON.
ports.restore: Writes a snapshot back as one commit. Safe to fire repeatedly; the snapshot is copied in, not consumed.
ports.snapshot: The captured snapshot, for persisting, transmitting, or feeding into another Restore.
ports.fullyRestorable: Whether this snapshot can be fully restored, or holds values captured only by reference.
ports.error: Carries a refused save or restore — an unknown store, or snapshot data that could not be read.

patterns: Save when a form opens, Restore on the Cancel button — a reset that needs no knowledge of the form's fields.
`snapshot` → JSON → persisted, then back through `snapshotData` on the next load, for state that survives a reload without a live store.
Attach a snapshot to a bug report so the state is reproducible rather than described.
antiPatterns: Using it for undo. It is a checkpoint, not a stack — State History keeps the ordered history.
Assuming a restore is total when `fullyRestorable` is false: keys in `byReferenceKeys` share their object with the snapshot.
Saving on every change. That is a history with extra steps, and unbounded — State History bounds itself.

ssr.note: Interval-based flushing needs a running timer, so it only happens in the browser. Add, Flush and size-based flushing behave normally.

inputs.name: flushInterval
inputs.description: Flush automatically this often while items are buffered. 0 disables interval flushing.

inputs.name: flushSize
inputs.description: Flush automatically once this many items are buffered. 0 disables size-based flushing.

inputs.name: maxSize
inputs.description: Hard cap on buffered items. Overflow drops the oldest and is reported on Dropped Items. 0 means no cap.

enrichment.summary: Stream Buffer: batches items arriving faster than the UI wants to react, flushing on a count, an interval, or on demand.
enrichment.description: Each `add` appends the current `data` to a buffer. The buffer empties when `flushSize` items have collected, when `flushInterval` milliseconds have passed since the first item after the last flush, or when `flush` fires — whichever comes first. `flushedData` is a detached array, so a later Add cannot mutate what a downstream node is already rendering. The interval timer is armed only while items are waiting, is re-armed rather than left stale when the interval changes, and is cleared on a manual flush and when the node is deleted. `maxSize` caps the buffer, dropping the oldest and reporting it on `droppedItems` with an `overflowed` signal.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any producer that outruns the UI: a token stream driving a Repeater, high-rate telemetry, a log feed. Batching turns hundreds of small graph updates a second into a few. Not needed when updates are already infrequent, and not a substitute for Text Accumulator when the thing being batched is text that should be concatenated rather than listed.

ports.data: The item to buffer on the next Add. Any type.
ports.add: Appends the current item. Wire the stream's message signal here.
ports.flushSize: Flush once this many items are buffered. 0 disables size-based flushing.
ports.flushInterval: Flush this many milliseconds after the buffer stops being empty. 0 disables interval flushing. Only fires in the browser, never during a server render.
ports.maxSize: Hard cap on buffered items. Overflow drops the oldest; 0 means no cap.
ports.flushedData: The batch released by the last flush — a fresh array each time.
ports.droppedItems: Running count of items lost to the cap. Non-zero means the consumer cannot keep up.
ports.flushed: Fires after each flush, once Flushed Data has updated.
ports.overflowed: Fires when the cap dropped items.

patterns: Server-Sent Events `onMessage` → `add` with `flushInterval` 250 and `flushedData` → For Each: a live list that repaints four times a second instead of hundreds.
`flushSize` and `flushInterval` together give 'whichever comes first', which keeps both a burst and a trickle responsive.
The stream's `onClose` → `flush` releases the tail of a batch that never reached the flush size.
antiPatterns: Relying on Flush Interval during server-side rendering — timers never advance there, so only Add, Flush and size-based flushing work.
Using this to concatenate streamed text; Text Accumulator is the node for that.
Setting Flush Size to 1, which is the same as no buffer at all plus an extra hop.

inputs.name: delimiter
inputs.description: Message boundary. Leave empty to accumulate everything without splitting — the mode a token stream wants.

inputs.name: maxLength
inputs.description: Cap on the pending buffer. Overflow drops the oldest characters and is reported on Dropped Characters.

inputs.name: maxMessages
inputs.description: Cap on retained complete messages; the oldest are dropped first. 0 keeps them all, which grows forever.

enrichment.summary: Text Accumulator: collects stream fragments into growing text, and splits complete messages off a delimiter.
enrichment.description: Each `add` appends the current `chunk` to a buffer. With an empty delimiter nothing is ever split and `accumulated` is simply the text so far — the mode a token stream wants. With a delimiter (newline by default) every complete piece moves to `messages` and only the unfinished tail stays in `accumulated`, so a message split across chunk boundaries reassembles correctly. Both stores are bounded: `maxLength` caps the pending buffer and `maxMessages` caps the retained list, dropping the oldest first and reporting the loss on `droppedCharacters` / `droppedMessages` plus an `overflowed` signal rather than growing without limit in a long-lived session. An empty chunk is ignored, so a stream's keep-alive frames do not fire `changed`.
enrichment.whenToUse: Assembling anything that arrives in pieces: AI tokens into a displayable answer, log lines out of a chunked feed, NDJSON lines before parsing them. Pair it with Server-Sent Events or any node that emits fragments. Not needed when each event is already a whole value — wire that straight to its consumer.

ports.chunk: The fragment to append. Text, numbers and booleans are accepted; an object or an array is refused and named on `error`, because it means a JSON-parsed `data` output was wired here where the stream's `text` output was wanted.
ports.add: Appends the current chunk. Wire the stream's `onMessage` here; the chunk value arrives first.
ports.delimiter: Message boundary. Empty means no boundaries — accumulate everything, which is what a token stream needs.
ports.maxLength: Cap on the pending buffer in characters. Overflow drops the oldest and reports it; 0 disables the cap.
ports.maxMessages: Cap on retained complete messages. 0 keeps them all, which grows forever in a long session.
ports.accumulated: The text not yet terminated by a delimiter. With no delimiter this is the whole stream so far.
ports.lastMessage: The most recent complete message, for the common case of only wanting the newest.
ports.byteCount: UTF-8 size of the pending buffer, which differs from Character Count for anything non-ASCII.
ports.changed: Fires on every non-empty Add, so a Text node repaints as the stream arrives.
ports.messageReceived: Fires once per Add that completed at least one message — not once per message.
ports.overflowed: Fires when a cap dropped data. Wire it if losing the oldest content matters.
ports.error: Empty until something that is not text arrives on `chunk`, then a message naming what came and which output to wire instead. Clears on the next usable chunk and on Clear.

patterns: Server-Sent Events `text` → `chunk`, `onMessage` → `add`, delimiter empty, `accumulated` → Text `text`: an answer that types itself out.
Delimiter `\n` with `messages` → For Each renders a growing log without re-parsing the whole buffer each time.
The stream's `onOpen` → `clear` resets the accumulator when a new response starts.
antiPatterns: Wiring a stream's `data` output into `chunk`. `data` is JSON-parsed and is an object for an OpenAI-style payload; wire `text` (with the stream's `textPath` set) or a Function node that picks out the string field.
Leaving `maxMessages` at 0 in a session that runs for hours — the array grows until the tab does.
Wiring `add` from a signal that fires before `chunk` is set (a Function's own output, say) — the last chunk gets appended twice and the newest not at all.

ssr.note: A WebSocket cannot be meaningfully opened during a server render and would leak a socket per request; the node connects in the browser after hydration.

inputs.name: autoConnect
inputs.description: Connect as soon as a URL is available, without waiting for a Connect signal.

inputs.name: heartbeatInterval
inputs.description: Send Heartbeat Message this often while open. 0 disables it. Only enable this if your server expects the message — it is application data, not a protocol ping frame.

inputs.name: heartbeatReply
inputs.description: Exact text the server answers a heartbeat with. It is measured as Latency, hidden from On Message, and — if it stops arriving — treated as a dead connection. Leave empty to only send heartbeats.

inputs.name: jitter
inputs.description: Spread reconnect attempts randomly across the second half of each backoff window.

inputs.name: maxQueueSize
inputs.description: Messages the queue holds before further Sends are refused and counted in Dropped. 0 or less means unlimited, which can grow without bound during a long outage.

inputs.name: maxRetries
inputs.description: Reconnect attempts allowed per outage. 0 disables retrying; a negative value means unlimited.

inputs.name: message
inputs.description: Value to send. Objects are JSON-serialized; ArrayBuffers and typed arrays are sent as binary frames.

inputs.name: messageType
inputs.description: Auto sends binary values as binary and everything else as text. Binary forces text and objects to be UTF-8 encoded first.

inputs.name: protocols
inputs.description: Comma-separated WebSocket subprotocols to offer during the handshake.

inputs.name: reconnectDelay
inputs.description: First backoff delay. Each further attempt doubles it, up to Max Reconnect Delay.

inputs.name: whenDisconnected
inputs.description: What a Send does while the connection is not open. Queue holds it (in order) until the socket reopens; Drop discards it and counts it; Report Error also sets Last Error and fires On Error.

enrichment.summary: Two-way WebSocket connection: send and receive text, JSON or binary, with connection state as graph outputs.
enrichment.description: A bidirectional transport for agent chat, collaboration, telemetry and any other stream where the client also talks back. `url` plus `autoConnect` opens the socket; `Connect`/`Disconnect` do it by hand. `Send` transmits whatever is on `message` — a string goes as text, an object is JSON-serialized, an ArrayBuffer or typed array goes as a binary frame, and `messageType: binary` UTF-8 encodes text first. Received text is JSON-parsed onto `received` with the original on `receivedRaw`; binary arrives on `received` as an ArrayBuffer with `receivedIsBinary` true. Everything about the connection's health is an output rather than a console message: `connectionState` moves through idle → connecting → open → reconnecting → closed/error, `retryCount` counts attempts within the current outage, `lastError` says what went wrong, `closeCode`/`closeReason` carry the server's own explanation, and `queueSize`/`droppedCount` account for every message that has not reached the wire. Reconnection is exponential backoff from `reconnectDelay`, doubling to `maxReconnectDelay`, with jitter, stopping after `maxRetries` — or immediately for close codes where retrying is futile (1002, 1003, 1007–1010, 1015). Giving up sets `connectionState` to error and fires `onError`; it is never silent.
enrichment.whenToUse: When the client needs to send as well as receive — chat with an agent, collaborative editing, live cursors, device control, order placement. If the server only pushes and the client never sends, Server-Sent Events is simpler and more firewall-friendly. This node is transport only: point it at your own endpoint, and use ordinary Object/Array/Function nodes to shape what flows through it. It is client-only, so it stays inert during server-side rendering and connects in the browser after hydration.

ports.url: Must start with ws:// or wss://. Anything else is rejected as an error rather than attempted. Use wss:// in production. Browsers cannot set WebSocket headers, so tokens go in the query string or in a first message sent from On Open.
ports.autoConnect: Connects as soon as a URL exists — no Connect signal needed. With no URL the node simply stays idle; an explicit Connect with no URL is reported as an error.
ports.protocols: Comma-separated subprotocols offered during the handshake. Changing this, like changing the URL, rebuilds the connection.
ports.autoReconnect: Reconnect after any close the app did not ask for, including a clean 1000 (a server closing an idle connection is the commonest reason to want reconnection). Turn it off and an abnormal close lands in the error state instead.
ports.maxRetries: Attempts allowed per outage. 0 never retries; a negative value retries forever. When the budget runs out, `connectionState` becomes error, `lastError` names the count, and `onError` fires.
ports.heartbeatInterval: Off by default. WebSocket protocol ping frames are unreachable from a browser, so this sends Heartbeat Message as ordinary application data — only enable it if your server expects that exact message.
ports.heartbeatReply: The exact text the server answers with. It is measured as `latency`, hidden from On Message, and — if a heartbeat goes a whole interval unanswered — treated as a dead connection, closing and reconnecting. TCP can hold a half-open socket for minutes, so this is the only way to notice one.
ports.whenDisconnected: Queue (default) holds sends in order until the socket reopens; Drop discards and counts them; Report Error also sets Last Error and fires On Error. Whichever you pick, nothing vanishes without appearing in `queueSize` or `droppedCount`.
ports.maxQueueSize: When the queue is full the newest send is refused, not the oldest evicted — the queue stays an ordered prefix of what the app tried to say. 0 or less means unlimited, which can grow without bound during a long outage.
ports.message: Value to send, read at the moment Send fires. Objects are JSON-serialized; ArrayBuffers, typed arrays and Blobs are sent as binary whatever Message Type says.
ports.connectionState: idle | connecting | open | reconnecting | closed | error. 'reconnecting' spans the whole outage — the wait and every attempt — so it is a single state to render, not a flicker.
ports.retryCount: Attempts made during the current outage; back to 0 on a successful open or a manual Connect.
ports.queueSize: Messages waiting for the socket to reopen.
ports.droppedCount: Messages that will never be sent: dropped by policy, refused by a full queue, failed to encode, or still queued when the node was deleted.
ports.latency: Round trip of the last answered heartbeat, in ms. Stays 0 unless both Heartbeat Interval and Heartbeat Reply are set.
ports.received: The parsed message. Valid JSON text becomes the value it describes; anything else stays a string; binary frames arrive as an ArrayBuffer.
ports.onMessage: Fires per received frame, after `received`/`receivedRaw` have updated. Heartbeat replies are transport bookkeeping and do not fire it.
ports.onMessageSent: Fires per message handed to the socket, including each one flushed from the queue. Heartbeats do not fire it.
ports.onReconnect: Fires on every open after the first. A WebSocket has no session resume, so a reconnect is a new session and the node cannot know what was missed — wire this to whatever re-fetches state, the way you would handle a resync.
ports.onClose: Fires whenever the socket goes down, including when a reconnect is about to be attempted; read `connectionState` to tell the two apart. A Connect that replaces a live socket does not fire it, because the app asked for that.
ports.onError: Fires for a rejected URL, a failed connect, a refused or failed send, a dead heartbeat, and the moment reconnection is abandoned.

patterns: `connectionState` → a status Text, and `lastError` → an error Text: an outage becomes something the user can see rather than a UI that has quietly stopped answering.
Leave `whenDisconnected` on Queue so a message typed during a reconnect is held in order and sent on reopen instead of lost.
`onOpen` → send an auth or subscribe frame: the queue is flushed after On Open, so the handshake always precedes the backlog.
`onReconnect` → re-fetch history or re-subscribe, since the new session replays nothing.
`droppedCount` → a Condition → a 'messages were lost' notice, for apps where silent loss is not acceptable.
antiPatterns: Assuming a message handed to Send arrived. `socket.send` only buffers, and a connection that dies before the frame leaves loses it with no way to say which — add application-level acknowledgements if that matters.
Turning on the heartbeat against a server that does not expect it: the message is ordinary application data and most servers will either ignore it or close the connection.
Using this where the client only listens — Server-Sent Events reconnects natively and passes through more firewalls.
Setting Max Queue Size to 0 on a long-lived page: an outage then grows the queue without bound.

Putting a long-lived secret in the URL. Browsers cannot set WebSocket headers, but a query-string token ends up in server logs; prefer a short-lived ticket, or authenticate with a first message from On Open.

ssr.note: The scheduler clock is frozen during server render; the value stays at its start and Finished never fires there.

enrichment.summary: Animate To Value: tweens its output toward whatever targetValue currently is, with duration, delay and easing.
enrichment.description: Animate To Value is the current general-purpose tween.
